snippet.title: Conquering Canada: The (Staggering) Siege of Quebec and the Fall of New France
snippet.description:
In 1759, the French Empire stood on the brink. Its American colony of New France was in peril. The British campaign of 1758 had shattered French control along the wilderness frontier. Thirteen Native nations—once firm French allies—had sworn not to fight for them under the Treaty of Easton. Most devastating of all, however, the fortress of Louisbourg had fallen after a grueling siege by General Jeffery Amherst, opening the St. Lawrence to a British invasion. Meanwhile, most of France’s resources were tied up in Europe, where the fronts of the Seven Years’ War had become deadlocked and hopes for a swift resolution on the continent’s battlefields were fading fast. Seizing the opportunity, Britain’s secretary of state, William Pitt, resolved to deliver a painful blow to France by stripping it of its colony. With the momentum on Britain’s side, he laid plans for an offensive that would drive the French from North America once and for all.

snippet.title: How Hard Was It to Supply Arrows to Archers in Battles?

snippet.title: True Size - Army of Joan of Arc (c.1430) DOCUMENTARY
snippet.description:
Watch the full documentary on Joan of Arc (and more) with HistoryAdventures https://youtube.com/@historyadventures-1?si=9Gnw0pkHq-MzyltD

In this history documentary we explore the True Size of the Army of Joan of Arc. This involves a review of the nature of the French Army as it entered the Hundred Years War. We cover its method of organization, equipment, and muster. The major phases of the war are then covered to highlight the changes to the military of medieval france. This includes casualties from battles like Crecy and Agincourt as well as the broader cullings of the Black Death. We then review the nature of the army of 1430 when Joan of Arc emerged to lead it. The documentary then covers the early campaigns of the maiden which culminates in the Siege of Orleans.

snippet.title: The King Who Defeated Rome… By Vanishing Underground ⚔️🏺
snippet.description:
Rome conquered nations, crushed rebellions, and broke kingdoms…
but one king refused to be caught — because he vanished into the earth itself.

This is the legendary story of Mithridates VI, Rome’s most dangerous enemy.
A ruler so elusive the Romans called him “The Eastern Hannibal.”

When Rome invaded his lands and sent entire legions to capture him, Mithridates didn’t flee…
He descended into a hidden world beneath the mountains — a vast network of tunnels, caverns, and underground cities.

From there, he waged a shadow-war that terrified Rome:
⚔️ Camps attacked from below
⚠️ Scouts disappearing
🔥 Explosions shaking the ground
🕳️ Entire patrols swallowed by the earth

For months Rome wasn’t fighting an army…
They were fighting a ghost.

snippet.title: Defining the Century: The (Staggering) Siege of Antwerp 1584/85 | Eighty Years' War
snippet.description:
Artwork from the channel collected into a coloring book (line art + colored versions):
https://amzn.to/4veRAb4
It also includes some illustrations that haven’t appeared in the videos yet.
(Disclosure: As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases.)

In 1584, the people of Antwerp made a drastic decision: they flooded the land surrounding their city. They resorted to this drastic measure because the Spanish general Alessandro Farnese was marching toward them with one goal—he was determined to conquer Antwerp. At the time, the city was not only a major economic hub but also the capital of the Dutch Revolt—the war for independence fought by the Dutch Republic against Spanish rule. For Farnese, stripping the insurgents of this vital stronghold would be the crowning achievement of a seven-year campaign against the rebellious provinces.
The siege of Antwerp was worthy of an epic film. To starve the city into submission, the Spanish built a massive bridge across the 900-meter-wide Scheldt River, cutting Antwerp off from the outside world. In a desperate attempt to free themselves from this iron grip, the defenders flooded the entire region, deployed fireships intending to destroy the bridge, and even built a colossal warship to break through and reconnect with their allies. The siege was one of the defining events of the century, and was closely followed by contemporary observers. Later, even the famous German poet Friedrich Schiller wrote an account of the events. This is how modern historiography tells the story of the staggering siege of Antwerp.

snippet.title: How Baldwin IV’s 500 Templars CRUSHED Saladin’s 30,000 at Montgisard
snippet.description:
In 1177, the Battle of Montgisard became one of the most extraordinary victories in medieval history. Barely five hundred Crusader knights under King Baldwin IV of Jerusalem faced more than thirty thousand soldiers of Saladin, the most powerful commander of the Ayyubid Empire and the rising force of the Crusades.
Outnumbered over sixty to one, the Leper King led a sudden downhill charge that smashed directly into Saladin’s unprepared vanguard, turning certain defeat into a decisive victory that saved Jerusalem from destruction.

This cinematic historical documentary tells the full story of the Battle of Montgisard 1177 how Baldwin IV rallied the Kingdom of Jerusalem, raised the True Cross, unified the Templar Knights, and launched a shock assault that shattered the core of Saladin’s army.
We explore the tactics, the terrain, the Crusader strategy, the collapse of the Ayyubid lines, and the moment Saladin himself was forced to flee the battlefield.

Against impossible odds, faith, discipline, and one of the greatest cavalry charges of the Middle Ages created a miracle that altered the course of the Crusades.
This is the legacy of Baldwin IV the king who should have died young, yet became the commander who defeated one of history’s greatest military leaders.

snippet.title: How 12 Men Stopped 700 Viking Longships — And Built a Tower Overnight to Prove It
snippet.description:
Paris. 885 AD. A fleet of Viking longships rows up the Seine — hundreds of ships, thousands of warriors, demanding gold or blood. The Franks refuse. The Vikings attack.
Catapults. Battering rams. Greek fire. By nightfall, the northeast tower is crumbling. The Vikings pull back and wait. By morning, they expect rubble and an open road into the city.
Instead, they find a second story.
Twelve defenders had worked through the freezing November night — under threat of attack, in the dark — and not only rebuilt the tower but raised it higher. The psychological blow shattered Viking confidence. Month after month of attacks, mining, and fire assaults followed. None of it broke Paris.
Then Emperor Charles the Fat arrived with his army. And paid anyway.
He granted the Vikings free passage upriver to raid Burgundy — everything Paris had bled to deny them, handed over by their own emperor. Count Odo, who had commanded the defense, never forgot. Three years later, he was King of France.
This is the siege that ended the Carolingian line and planted the seed of a new kingdom.

snippet.title: The Battle of Mansurah (1250) When the Nile Drowned a Crusade
snippet.description:
In 1250, on the banks of the Nile, a Crusade met not only an army — but a river.

This video respectfully explores the dramatic Battle of Mansurah, where the Seventh Crusade, led by King Louis IX of France, faced the fierce resistance of the Ayyubids and the rising Mamluks in Egypt. What began as a bold campaign to strike at the heart of the Islamic world turned into one of the most devastating defeats in Crusader history.

In this video, discover how:
• The Crusaders captured Damietta and advanced confidently into the Nile Delta
• The flooded Nile and Egypt’s terrain became silent but deadly allies
• The Mamluk commanders used strategy, deception, and urban warfare in Mansurah
• Robert of Artois’ reckless assault led to catastrophe inside the city
• King Louis IX was captured — shocking all of Europe
• The battle reshaped the balance of power in the eastern Mediterranean

Through strategy, environment, and human ambition, the Battle of Mansurah reveals how overconfidence, geography, and local resistance can overturn even the mightiest armies.

What do you think was the decisive factor — the Nile, leadership mistakes, or Mamluk strategy? Share your thoughts in the comments, and don’t forget to subscribe for more in-depth historical explorations.

snippet.title: When Richard the Lionheart’s 7,000 CRUSHED Saladin’s 30,000
snippet.description:
In 1191, during the Third Crusade, Richard the Lionheart, King of England, led just 7,000 Crusaders into the Holy Land, facing Saladin’s army of over 30,000. Outnumbered and exhausted, Richard the Lionheart confronted the full strength of a united Islamic empire in one of the most decisive clashes of medieval history. The campaign would culminate in the Battle of Arsuf, a turning point in the struggle between Christian Europe and the Islamic world.

Marching along the Levantine coast, Saladin’s forces harassed the Crusader column relentlessly, launching constant cavalry attacks in an effort to break formation. At Arsuf, the moment finally came. After hours of sustained assault, the Crusader army held its ground until Richard the Lionheart ordered the counter-charge. The result shattered Saladin’s field army and forced a retreat, reshaping the balance of power in the Holy Land.

This cinematic historical documentary explores Richard the Lionheart vs Saladin, the Battle of Arsuf, and the brutal reality of warfare during the Crusades. It is a story of leadership, discipline, and faith — when the survival of the Crusader states, and Europe’s future in the East, depended on a single command.

Chapters:
00:00 – Christendom on the Brink
02:50 – Richard Lands and the March Begins
06:59 – Arsuf: Saladin’s Full Assault
16:48 – Victory, Aftermath, and Legacy

snippet.title: Why the Assyrians Inflated Goats Before Battle
snippet.description:
Carved into the walls of King Ashurnasirpal II's palace at Nimrud around 865 BC is one of the most ingenious military details of the ancient world: Assyrian soldiers crossing a river using inflated animal skins as personal flotation devices.

The skins — made from goat or sheep — kept weapons dry and allowed the army to cross deep water with no bridge and no ford, appearing on riverbanks the enemy believed were unreachable.

Horses swam alongside, guided by their riders. Chariots and siege engines were dismantled and ferried across on rafts buoyed by dozens of inflated skins, known as keleks — a technology still used on the Tigris and Euphrates into modern times.

While their enemies treated rivers as defensive walls, the Assyrians treated them as open roads.

The relief survives today in the British Museum. #Assyria #AncientHistory #Archaeology #Nimrud #Shorts #HistoryShorts #TimelineHistory

snippet.title: Why Assyria's Generals Could Never Have Sons
snippet.description:
The most powerful generals in the Assyrian empire had one thing in common: none of them could ever have a son. For generations, the deadliest threat to an Assyrian king wasn't a foreign army — it was his own governors, who could raise their banner and try to found a dynasty of their own. So Tiglath-Pileser III handed the provinces and the armies to eunuchs, the sha reshe — men who could never have heirs, and so could never build a dynasty to rival the crown. It held the empire's center stable for over a century.

snippet.title: "A Production Line of Death”: How Volley Fire Changed the Face of Battle (and Where it Originated)
snippet.description:
Thanks to Opera for sponsoring this video. Click here https://opr.as/Opera-browser-sandrhomanhistory to upgrade your browser for FREE!

When firing volleys, all men of the first row of a formation shot simultaneously. Then, they made way for their comrades to fire the next round. Volley fire emerged in the 16th century and fundamentally changed warfare. It enabled infantry with arquebuses and muskets to fire continuously for the first time in history, making fighting in formation more efficient—and battles more deadly. How this firing mode looked in its final form can be seen, for example, in the film Zulu, which depicts the Battle of Rorke’s Drift in 1879.  In this battle, 139 British soldiers defended a mission station in South Africa against almost 4,000 Zulu warriors. Thanks to the deliberate use of volley fire, they managed to repel several assaults and hold the station. This video explores how and where volley fire originated, how it worked, and why it was so effective.

In early March 1579, a Spanish army advanced on the Dutch city of Maastricht. This marked the beginning of a 111-day siege, characterized by bloody assaults, intense mine warfare, and massive construction efforts—including a 20-meter-high artillery platform. The defenders were so determined to hold the city that even after the enemy breached the walls, they fought on and built an entire secondary earthen rampart inside.
Maastricht was one of the most important fortresses in the region due to its position on the border river Maas. It had long served as a Spanish stronghold after they gained control of the Netherlands in 1556, but in 1577 it fell to the Dutch, who used it in their uprising against the Spanish crown. King Philipp II was determined to reassert his authority—and reconquer Maastricht. To achieve this, he dispatched one of the most capable generals of the time—Alessandro Farnese, the future Duke of Parma. Maastricht now faced the most formidable opponent the Dutch revolt had ever encountered.
